stories.title: Insurance Is Taking a Bigger Bite Out of Apartment Revenue
stories.excerpt: In 2019, a Louisiana apartment property financed in a commercial mortgage-backed securities or Freddie K-Series deal spent about $4.77 on insurance for every $100 of revenue it collected. By 2025, that figure was $9.42, and that is after premiums fell last year. The Louisiana example underscores the shape of the apartment insurance story. After five straight years of increases, insurance costs on apartment properties fell 2.2 percent in 2025, according to CRED iQ’s same-store analysis of property operating statements. That followed a 28.5 percent jump in 2023. But the relief came off a much higher base: Apartment insurance costs are still more than double their 2019 level. The pressure has clearly eased. In 2023, 46 percent of apartment properties saw their premiums rise more than 20 percent. In 2025, 24 percent experienced that 20 percent increase, and 36 percent paid less than the year before. The Sun Belt turned first The markets with the sharpest run-up are the ones now getting relief. Florida apartment premiums rose 2.5 fold between 2019 and 2024, including a 46 percent jump in 2023 alone. In 2025 they fell 9.8 percent. Texas apartments’ insurance rates fell 8.4 percent, and Louisiana apartments saw a 10.5 percent drop last year. Nearly two-thirds of Florida apartment properties paid less than a year earlier, as did 57 percent in Texas and 58 percent in Louisiana. The decline has continued into 2026. In the first half of the year, 59 percent of apartment properties paid less for insurance than in the first half of 2025, up from 38 percent a year earlier. In the Sun Belt, 72 percent paid less, and the typical premium fell 11 percent. Coastal apartment owners have not shared in the relief. Premiums on apartments in major coastal metros rose 4.8 percent in 2025, and premiums for California apartments rose 6.3 percent. California has now passed Florida on cumulative growth since 2019, with an index of 251 against Florida’s 230, and coastal apartments overall (226)
bullets: Louisiana apartment insurance costs rose from $4.77 to $9.42 per $100 revenue (2019–2025).
Florida premiums fell 9.8% in 2025 after 2.5x increase since 2019; Texas down 8.4%.
2025 relief modest: 24% of properties saw >20% premium increases vs. 46% in 2023.
stories.summary: Apartment insurance costs have nearly doubled since 2019 despite a 2.2% decline in 2025. Florida and Texas—markets hit hardest by premium spikes (2.5x and similar magnitude jumps)—are finally seeing meaningful relief, though absolute costs remain elevated. The shift suggests insurers are repricing and stabilizing after five years of acute increases driven by climate risk and litigation.
stories.impact: Cost moderation in high-risk markets (Florida, Texas, Louisiana) reduces developer underwriting drag and improves stabilized NOI, making new construction and value-add acquisitions more viable. However, insurance still running 100%+ above 2019 levels means elevated operating costs persist in sunbelt markets—factor this into pro forma assumptions and cap rate spreads for Florida and Texas multifamily.

stories.title: Brooklyn Apartment Leasing Strongest Since 2020 for a September: Report
stories.excerpt: Apartments are filling up in Brooklyn. Leasing momentum in Brooklyn’s rental market increased 10 percent annually in September, as the borough notched its strongest September of apartment leasing activity since 2020 at 1,407 leases signed, according to data from the Corcoran Group. Manhattan, on the other hand, had a somewhat shabby September. Apartment leasing activity in the borough declined 5 percent year-over-year to 3,841 leases signed, the data found. And renters are continuing to face a shortage in available Manhattan pads. “The number of available apartments [in Manhattan] reached its lowest September level since 2019, while the vacancy rate held near 1.5 percent, highlighting just how challenging the market remains for renters,” Gary Malin, chief operating officer at The Corcoran Group, wrote in the report. “With demand continuing to outpace supply, competition remains frustratingly intense across much of the borough.” Rents in both boroughs grew on a year-over-year basis, according to the Corcoran data. Brooklyn saw a 5 percent year-over-year rise in rent for September to an average of $4,300 per month, while Manhattan’s average rent shot up 9 percent year-over-year to $5,395 per month. There were 3,428 active apartment listings in Brooklyn during September, a decline of 11 percent when compared to August 2026 and a drop of 25 percent year-over-year. In Manhattan, there were 5,015 active listings, down 2 percent from August and 16 percent from September 2025. Brooklyn’s uptick in leasing activity in September was driven by leasing for two-bedroom apartments, which saw 21 percent growth year-over-year to 434 leases — the highest September total since 2020 — and studio signings, which sat at 248 leases, representing the strongest September on record for that unit type, according to Corcoran. bullets: Brooklyn September 2025 leasing up 10% YoY to 1,407 units; strongest September since 2020.
Manhattan leasing down 5% YoY to 3,841 units; vacancy near 1.5% with lowest available inventory since 2019.
Brooklyn rents +5% YoY to $4,300/mo avg; Manhattan rents rising but supply severely constrained.
stories.summary: Brooklyn's rental market is accelerating while Manhattan faces acute supply scarcity and intensifying competition for limited units. Brooklyn achieved its best September leasing since 2020 (up 10% YoY), while Manhattan's leasing declined 5% YoY despite persistent rent growth, indicating demand far exceeds available stock. Manhattan's vacancy near 1.5% and inventory at nine-year lows signal a bifurcation in outer-borough strength.
stories.impact: Brooklyn is re-emerging as the stronger lease-up and rent-growth engine; this signals a multi-year opportunity window for new supply delivery in Brooklyn's underbuilt submarkets (Williamsburg, Park Slope, Sunset Park). Manhattan's supply crunch and high vacancy floor suggest limited room for new Class A starts absent major relocations; focus capital on Brooklyn and Queens development to capture the demand migration outward.

stories.title: AI Spurs Unprecedented Proptech Interest, Along with Questions (VIDEO)
stories.excerpt: “With the emergence of AI, I’ve never seen so much interest in technology,” said Michael Beckerman, founder and CEO of CREtech, the largest global conference company devoted to technological innovation in the built world. “”So we’re getting more real estate companies coming to CRE Tech than ever before.” With that heightened interest, though, “there’s a tremendous amount of uncertainty as to what’s the path” in utilizing AI, Beckerman continued. “Do we adopt a solution, a startup, a tech solution that’s off the shelf? Do we build something ourselves using Claude or Gemini or OpenAI? Or is it a combination of the two? So the good news is more interest than ever.” In advance of CREtech New York, set for Oct. 20-21 at the Javits Center in Manhattan, Beckerman sat down with Daniel Ceniceros, cofounder and CEO of Connect Media, to discuss the current state of proptech. In the video below, you’ll glean insights into the level of investment in proptech and the long-term implications of AI adoption for commercial real estate firms and their employees. The post AI Spurs Unprecedented Proptech Interest, Along with Questions (VIDEO) appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: CREtech founder reports unprecedented proptech interest driven by AI adoption across real estate.
Real estate firms face strategic uncertainty: buy off-shelf vs. build custom vs. hybrid AI solutions.
CREtech New York conference Oct. 20–21 at Javits Center signals high vendor and operator engagement.
stories.summary: AI adoption is spurring record proptech interest and investment, but real estate companies are uncertain on implementation strategy—whether to acquire vendor solutions, build internally, or blend approaches. CREtech founder Beckerman notes this is the highest level of technology sector engagement he has seen.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily development (not about demand, supply, capital, or construction cost). This is an operational/tech adoption story relevant to asset management and leasing efficiency post-completion, not to the development underwriting or pipeline.

stories.title: C-PACE Financing Can Be a Useful Part of a Data Center’s Capital Stack
stories.excerpt: The data center boom faces a financing challenge: Developers must fund not only the buildings themselves, but also the power, cooling and other infrastructure required to support increasingly energy-intensive computing. The International Energy Agency estimates that data centers consumed approximately 415 terawatt hours of electricity globally in 2024, and it projects that consumption will more than double to approximately 945 terawatt hours by 2030, with artificial intelligence the most important driver of that growth. A $100 million Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy (C-PACE) financing for Patmos Hosting’s AI data center campus in Kansas City, Mo., illustrates one potential source of capital for that infrastructure. Glenn Miller (left) and Abraham Salandar. PHOTOS: Courtesy Katten Muchin Rosenman The loan, originated by PACE Loan Group through Missouri’s Show Me PACE program, was structured to fund equipment, HVAC and plumbing improvements supporting the cooling and electrical load of the 421,112-square-foot, 35-megawatt facility in the former Kansas City Star building. The transaction was the largest C-PACE deal in Missouri history, and was described as one of the first C-PACE loans in the country for a data center. According to the lender, many of the conversion costs were eligible, and the long-duration capital was well aligned with the sponsor’s business plan. Another example is the $40 million C-PACE financing, arranged through Texas’ Lone Star PACE program with capital from Nuveen Green Capital, for the conversion of a 774,000-square-foot facility at ViVa Center into a data center. (VivaVa Center is VivaVerse Solutions’ 2.3 million-square-foot technology hub on the former Compaq and Hewlett-Packard Enterprise campus in Houston.) The financing represents a 24 percent loan-to-value ratio and will fund energy-efficient windows, LED lighting, advanced HVAC systems and high-efficiency plumbing. bullets: Patmos Hosting secured $100M C-PACE financing for 35-MW AI data center in Kansas City, Mo.
IEA projects global data center electricity consumption doubles from 415 to 945 TWh by 2030 (AI-driven).
C-PACE structures infrastructure financing (HVAC, cooling, power) alongside building; alternative to traditional debt.
stories.summary: Data centers face mounting capital requirements to fund not only buildings but also power and cooling infrastructure. A $100M C-PACE deal for Patmos Hosting's Kansas City AI campus shows how Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy financing can fund equipment and mechanical systems alongside the structure. Global data center energy consumption is projected to more than double by 2030, driven primarily by AI.
stories.impact: Not directly relevant to multifamily development. However, the data center boom and energy-infrastructure financing innovation (C-PACE) could indirectly reduce construction labor and materials availability in markets with heavy data center buildout (Kansas City, Ashburn VA, Phoenix), potentially raising multifamily construction costs in those metros.

stories.title: Japanese Restaurant Udon Shin to Open First NYC Spot at 37 West 17th Street
stories.excerpt: Udon Shin, a popular Japanese restaurant with only two other U.S. locations, is gearing up to open its first New York City eatery, Commercial Observer has learned. Udon Shin has signed a 10-year, 2,500-square-foot lease at 37 West 17th Street in Manhattan’s Flatiron District, according to tenant broker Aaron Gavios of Gavios Realty Group. Asking rent was $30,000 per month for the space previously occupied by now-closed Italian restaurant Basta Pasta. Udon Shin originated in Tokyo but recently opened its first U.S. location in Mesa, Ariz., where its lines are “out the door,” Gavios said. Another U.S. spot is coming soon to Utah. “We are expecting long waits and long lines when Udon Shin opens here in the Flatiron District. It should be the latest Japanese foodie sensation,” Gavios said. Landlord the Moinian Group was represented in this deal by Samuel Chera and David Green of KSR. “The continued interest from exciting international restaurant concepts speaks to the strength of Manhattan’s retail market and the demand for quality locations,” Green said to CO. “We believe Udon Shin will be a great addition to the neighborhood and look forward to seeing its success.” Built in 1900, 37 West 17th Street is a seven-story office and commercial property two blocks west of Union Square Park and about six blocks south of the landmark Flatiron Building. Other tenants include acupuncture clinic the Yinova Center and British music producer De Wolfe Music USA. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Japanese restaurant Udon Shin signed 10-yr lease, 2,500 SF at 37 West 17th St, Manhattan Flatiron.
Asking rent $30k/mo ($144/SF/yr); replaces closed Basta Pasta; tenant has only two prior U.S. locations.
Broker notes high demand expectations and 'long lines' model; Moinian Group landlord; KSR and Gavios represented.
stories.summary: Udon Shin, a Tokyo-origin Japanese restaurant with minimal U.S. footprint, is anchoring a 2,500-SF Flatiron space at $30k/month. The deal signals strong landlord confidence in experiential retail and international food concepts in Manhattan's premium retail corridors, where rents remain robust despite office headwinds.
stories.impact: Minimal impact on multifamily development. Illustrates retail tenant confidence in Manhattan's Flatiron/SoHo—a signal of stable foot traffic and mixed-use vitality—which can support ground-floor retail at multifamily projects in the area, but does not affect residential demand, supply, or financing.

stories.title: Chef-Led Pacific Pearl Concept Opens at Irvine Company’s Newport Gateway
stories.excerpt: Irvine Company announced that Pacific Pearl Café, the chef-led concept from Chef Michael Campbell, has opened at Newport Gateway. Located at 19800 MacArthur Blvd. in a reimagined dining space, this is Pacific Pearl Café’s third Orange County location and first with Irvine Company. Located on the Concourse Level, Pacific Pearl Café serves breakfast and lunch Monday through Friday from 7:30 a.m. to 4 p.m, with happy hour launching soon. Pacific Pearl Café is part of a broader investment in Newport Gateway’s dining offerings, with an all-new space designed to serve customers throughout the day. “Pacific Pearl brings a new level of dining to Newport Gateway, with the quality and care of a chef-led restaurant available right in the workplace,” said Roger DeWames, president of Irvine Company Office Properties. “Michael has built a menu around high-quality ingredients and thoughtful preparation, giving our customers a great dining option throughout the day.” The post Chef-Led Pacific Pearl Concept Opens at Irvine Company’s Newport Gateway appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Pacific Pearl Café (Chef Michael Campbell) opened at Irvine Company's Newport Gateway, Orange County, Ca.
Third OC location, first with Irvine Co.; chef-led concept; weekday breakfast/lunch, happy hour planned.
Reflects Irvine Co. investment in workplace dining and experiential office amenities at Newport Gateway.
stories.summary: Irvine Company has opened a chef-led café at its Newport Gateway office property, marking the third local location for Pacific Pearl. The move highlights landlord investment in elevated workplace dining and amenity-rich office repositioning to attract and retain tenants.
stories.impact: No material impact on multifamily development. This is an office property amenity story; irrelevant to apartment demand, supply, capital, or construction.

stories.title: Walker Webcast: Willy Walker on the Risks, Missed Opportunities and Lessons That Shaped His Career
stories.excerpt: The 300th episode of the Walker Webcast, which aired Oct. 14, featured Walker & Dunlop Chairman and CEO Willy Walker as the interviewee, rather than the one asking the questions. In the hour-long question-and-answer session hosted by The New Yorker’s political reporter Evan Osnos (and driven by submitted audience questions), Walker discussed risks, missed opportunities and leadership lessons that helped drive his career. A Risky Acquisition In 2012, Walker & Dunlop negotiated the acquisition of a company owned by a private equity firm. As three bankers at the company brought in most of the revenue, “we said we would like to have a force majeure clause in the purchase and sale agreement that says that if these three bankers don’t come across in the acquisition, we can back out of the deal,” Walker said. The seller’s response? “The private equity firm that was selling us the company said, ‘that’s on you,’” Walker said. The situation presented a dilemma. Without those three bankers, Walker & Dunlop risked acquiring a company that could immediately lose nearly half its revenue. However, Walker persuaded his board to proceed, only to learn that on the day of the closing, a major competitor “put a massive amount of money on the table for those three bankers to move across to our competitive firm,” according to Walker. “I said, ‘Oh. I may have made a mistake.’” But during escrow, Walker & Dunlop encouraged the bankers to join the firm, and they did. “They’re still here today,” Walker said. He acknowledged that from a legal or board-of-directors standpoint, the deal might not have made sense. Walker said he had confidence in his team and its ability to retain the bankers to move forward with the transaction. “Unless you’re willing to take those types of risks, you’re not going to be able to create the type of growth and value that we have created,” he said. bullets: Walker & Dunlop CEO Willy Walker recounts 2012 risky acquisition with key-person concentration risk.
Deal closed despite lack of force majeure protection; bankers retained post-close; leadership paid off.
Walker Webcast 300th episode; discusses career risk-taking, strategic judgment, and board confidence.

Walker pushed the board to proceed despite the hazard; the bankers stayed on and remain with the firm, validating the bet on team retention and culture.

stories.title: University of Cambridge Chooses West Harlem Factory District for First U.S. Innovation Cohort
stories.excerpt: Cambridge Enterprise, the innovation arm of the University of Cambridge, has chosen West Harlem’s Factory District for the first U.S. outpost of its new Leap program, establishing a new pipeline that will bring Cambridge Enterprise companies to New York to pursue investors, customers, clinical relationships and opportunities for growth in the American market. The inaugural New York Leap cohort includes five Cambridge Enterprise portfolio companies spanning the fields of brain cancer, multiple sclerosis and CNS therapeutics, aging-related disease, tumor measurement and integrated photonics. They include Verinnogen, Streamtrix, Aila Biotech, Senesys.Bio and Wave Photonics. The companies will be based in Janus Property Company’s West Harlem Factory District, where they will utilize lab and office space and benefit from the specialized facilities and concentration of research institutions and startups of Innovation Triangle, as well as introductions to investors and potential commercial and clinical partners. The West Harlem outpost represents the second Leap cohort, following one in London. The post University of Cambridge Chooses West Harlem Factory District for First U.S. Innovation Cohort appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: University of Cambridge chose West Harlem Factory District for first U.S. Leap innovation cohort.
Five Cambridge portfolio companies in biotech/medtech (brain cancer, MS, photonics, aging) based at Janus Property Co.
West Harlem outpost leverages Innovation Triangle research cluster; second Leap cohort globally after London.
stories.summary: Cambridge Enterprise launched its first U.S. Leap accelerator cohort in West Harlem's Factory District, housing five biotech and medtech portfolio companies. The placement signals Cambridge's confidence in West Harlem's emerging innovation ecosystem and proximity to research institutions, positioning the area as a secondary biotech/tech hub.
stories.impact: West Harlem is consolidating a research and life-sciences identity around the Innovation Triangle (Columbia, CUMC, biotech startups), which could drive demand for specialized lab/office space and adjacent housing. Monitor for future academic-anchored residential development targeting young scientists and researchers in Upper Manhattan; potential upside for mixed-use or studio/1-BR multifamily near these clusters.

stories.title: Digital Communications Firm Next 15 Signs 6K-SF Lease at 78 Crosby Street
stories.excerpt: A U.K.-based digital communications firm has leased the third floor of a SoHo office building, Commercial Observer has learned. Next Fifteen Communications Group, also known as Next 15, signed a 6,350-square-foot lease at Milkystar’s 78 Crosby Street, the same building occupied by betting platform Polymarket, according to landlord broker Judson CRE. It will be the artificial intelligence-driven company’s first New York City office. Judson CRE declined to disclose the length of the lease but said the asking rent in the space was $75 per square foot. Nicholas Judson, Wendy McDonald and Crosby Matthews of Judson CRE negotiated on behalf of the landlord. Brandon DeGraff and Jimmy Giattino with Cushman & Wakefield represented the tenant when the deal closed in the last two weeks, but have since gone to work for JLL. C&W declined to comment while JLL did not immediately respond to request for comment. Polymarket moved into the SoHo building between Spring and Prince streets in 2023, occupying the fifth floor before expanding to 12,700 square feet on the fourth floor in August under its parent company, Blockratize. Both were founded by 28-year-old CEO and billionaire Shayne Coplan. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: U.K. digital firm Next 15 signed 6,350-SF lease, third floor, 78 Crosby St, SoHo, Manhattan.
Asking rent $75/SF/yr; first NYC office for AI-driven firm; same building houses Polymarket (2023 arrival).
Landlord Milkystar; JLL/Cushman & Wakefield represented tenant; deal closed last two weeks.
stories.summary: Next Fifteen Communications, a U.K.-based AI-driven digital firm, leased 6,350 SF in SoHo at $75/SF/yr. This is their first NYC office and sits in a building already housing crypto/fintech tenant Polymarket, signaling continued SoHo appeal for tech and AI-focused firms seeking premium office space.
stories.impact: Reinforces SoHo's attraction for AI/tech tenants and premium office. Minimal direct multifamily impact; however, concentration of AI and fintech startups in SoHo could lift adjacent residential demand among high-income young professionals, supporting rents in Lower Manhattan/Nolita/Downtown multifamily projects.

stories.title: Slatt Capital Arranges Life Company Refi for Palm Springs Retail
stories.excerpt: Slatt Capital arranged a $12,000,000 refinance for Gene Autry Plaza, a 60,629-square-foot multi-tenant retail property located in Palm Springs. Built in 2009, the property was financed through a life insurance company with a five-year term and 30-year amortization schedule. The permanent loan is structured as partial recourse. Michael Kaplan, Slatt Capital’s president, led the transaction on behalf of the unnamed borrower, with support from Andrew Friedeberg. Upland-based 1st Commercial Realty Group provides property management services for the asset, which is occupied by a mix of tenants including food, fitness and health operators. “Gene Autry Plaza checks a lot of boxes for lenders: a grocery-anchored center in an affluent market, with the daily-needs tenants that drive consistent foot traffic regardless of the economic cycle,” said Kaplan. “Life companies value that kind of durable, necessity-driven income, and the property’s location next to the Palm Springs Airport and the Gene Autry Business District adds to its appeal.” The post Slatt Capital Arranges Life Company Refi for Palm Springs Retail appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Slatt Capital arranged $12M refi for Gene Autry Plaza, 60.6k SF retail, Palm Springs, CA.
Built 2009, grocery-anchored, multi-tenant (food, fitness, health); life insurance company lender, 5yr term, 30yr amort.
Partial recourse structure; strong appeal to life cos. driven by daily-needs anchors and consistent cash flow.
stories.summary: Gene Autry Plaza, a 60,000+ SF grocery-anchored retail property in Palm Springs, closed a $12M life insurance company refinance on a five-year term with 30-year amortization. The property's necessity-driven tenant mix and proximity to Palm Springs Airport made it attractive to long-term life company capital seeking stable, inflation-resistant income.
stories.impact: No impact on multifamily development. This is a retail asset refi story; illustrates life company appetite for grocery-anchored centers but does not signal changes in residential capital, demand, supply, or development feasibility.
